questions.s: Commerce is best described as
o: trade together with the aids to trade
the making of goods in factories
the extraction of raw materials from nature
buying and selling of goods only
questions.e: Commerce covers trade (buying and selling) plus the services that help it, such as banking, transport, insurance, warehousing and advertising. Buying and selling alone is trade, which is only one part of commerce.

questions.s: Which hindrance of trade is removed by transport?
questions.e: Goods are produced in one place and consumed in another; transport carries them across that distance, removing the hindrance of place. The hindrance of time is removed by warehousing, which stores goods until they are needed.

questions.s: Warehousing removes which hindrance of trade?
questions.e: Goods are often produced in one season and consumed throughout the year. Warehouses store them until demand arises, bridging the gap of time. Distance (place) is the job of transport, not warehousing.

questions.s: Insurance is an aid to trade because it
o: removes every possible risk of fire, theft and accident from a business
supplies the trader with working capital
moves goods from producers to consumers
spreads the loss of a few among many who face the same risk
questions.e: Insurance cannot prevent fire or theft; it collects premiums from many people facing a risk and compensates the few who actually suffer the loss. Saying it removes every risk is the common mistake: the risk remains, only its financial burden is shared.

questions.s: Trade carried on between buyers and sellers within the boundaries of one country is called
questions.e: Home (internal) trade takes place within one country, for example between a Faisalabad mill and a Lahore shop. Entrepot and re-export trade both involve goods crossing national borders.

questions.s: Importing goods from one country in order to export them to another country is known as
questions.e: Entrepot (re-export) trade means goods are imported, sometimes processed or repacked, and then sent on to a third country. Plain export trade sells home-produced goods abroad, not goods first brought in from outside.

questions.s: The main difference between wholesale and retail trade is that a wholesaler usually
o: sells for cash while retailers sell on credit
sells only imported goods to the public
deals in only one product while a retailer usually stocks many different products
sells in large quantities to retailers rather than to final consumers
questions.e: A wholesaler buys in bulk from producers and sells in fairly large lots to retailers; the retailer then sells small quantities to consumers. Wholesalers often give credit to retailers, so the cash-versus-credit idea is false.

questions.s: Which of the following is a service provided by a wholesaler to manufacturers?
o: giving free after-sales repair service at each final consumer's home
selling small quantities to final consumers
buying goods in bulk and relieving them of storage
displaying goods in an attractive shop window
questions.e: By placing large orders and holding the stock, the wholesaler frees manufacturers from storing finished goods and from finding many small buyers. Selling small quantities to consumers is the retailer's role.

questions.s: "Breaking the bulk" in trade refers to
o: dividing large consignments into smaller lots for resale
refusing to buy goods in large quantities
separating damaged or broken goods from a shipment before it is sold
questions.e: Producers sell in bulk; wholesalers and retailers break these large quantities into lots small enough for the next buyer. It has nothing to do with damaged goods or machinery.

questions.s: A retailer is best described as
o: the last link between producers and consumers
a trader who sells only to other businesses
the first link between producers and wholesalers
an agent who never takes ownership of goods
questions.e: The retailer sells directly to the final consumer, so he is the last link in the chain of distribution. Selling only to other businesses describes a wholesaler.

questions.s: A large shop with separate sections for clothing, furniture, toys and groceries under one roof and one management is a
questions.e: A departmental store groups many departments in one building under a single management. A chain (multiple) store is the reverse arrangement: many branches in different places selling similar goods under one owner.

questions.s: Several shops in different cities, all owned by one firm, selling the same type of goods at uniform prices, are called
questions.e: Multiple shops, also called chain stores, are branches of one business spread over different areas, with standard goods and prices. A departmental store is one large building with many sections, not many branches.

questions.s: A hawker who moves from street to street selling goods from a cart is an example of a
questions.e: Itinerant retailers have no fixed place of business and move to reach customers, as hawkers and pedlars do. Fixed-shop retailers sell from permanent premises.

questions.s: In mail-order business, the seller and buyer mainly deal with each other through
o: face-to-face bargaining in a weekly market
auctions held at the seller's premises
catalogues, post or online orders with delivery to the buyer
a broker who keeps all the goods in his own warehouse until the buyer collects them
questions.e: Mail-order sellers advertise through catalogues or online listings, receive orders by post or electronically, and deliver goods to the buyer; there is no personal contact at a shop. Bargaining in a market is a feature of fixed or periodic markets, not mail order.

questions.s: A supermarket is mainly characterised by
o: home delivery of every order by salesmen who visit customers each week
self-service, with customers picking goods and paying at checkouts
credit sales to all regular customers
sale of only one line of goods at high prices
questions.e: In a supermarket, goods are displayed on open shelves, customers serve themselves and pay at a checkout; this keeps staff costs and prices low. Selling one line of goods describes a single-line or specialty shop.

questions.s: A written request from a buyer to a seller to supply stated goods on stated terms is
questions.e: The buyer sends an order to say exactly what he wants and on what terms. A quotation goes the other way: from seller to buyer, stating prices and terms before any order is placed.

questions.s: The document a seller sends to a prospective buyer stating the prices and terms on which goods can be supplied is a
questions.e: A quotation answers a buyer's enquiry with prices, discounts and delivery terms. Debit and credit notes adjust an amount after a sale has taken place.

questions.s: An invoice is a document that
o: is sent by the seller with details of goods sold and the amount due
gives the buyer legal ownership of goods while they are still at sea on a ship
is sent by the buyer to correct an earlier order
is issued by a bank to guarantee payment
questions.e: An invoice lists the goods sent, quantities, prices, discounts and the total payable, and is prepared by the seller. A bank's guarantee of payment is a letter of credit, not an invoice.

questions.s: A pro forma invoice differs from an ordinary invoice because it
o: is prepared by the buyer's bank, not the seller
is sent before a sale is completed and does not demand payment
records the goods returned by the buyer to the seller after the sale is complete
is sent only after the buyer has fully paid
questions.e: A pro forma invoice shows what an invoice would contain if the order were placed; it is used for quotations, advance payment or consignment, and it creates no debt. Goods returned are dealt with by a credit note.

questions.s: A seller finds that he undercharged a customer by Rs. 2,500 in an invoice. To correct this he should send the customer a
questions.e: A debit note tells the buyer that his account has been debited with an extra amount, as when he was undercharged. A credit note is the opposite: it reduces the buyer's debt, as for an overcharge or goods returned.

questions.s: When a buyer returns damaged goods, the seller sends him a
questions.e: Returned goods reduce what the buyer owes, so the seller credits the buyer's account and informs him with a credit note. A debit note would increase the buyer's debt.

questions.s: A document sent periodically by a supplier summarising all invoices, payments and returns for a customer, and showing the balance due, is a
questions.e: A statement of account, usually sent monthly, summarises the transactions of the period and the closing balance. A delivery note only accompanies goods to list what has been delivered.

questions.s: The letters E. & O.E. printed at the foot of an invoice mean that
o: the invoice has been examined and officially endorsed
the goods have been sent at the buyer's own risk
the seller may correct any errors or omissions later
the price includes all export and other expenses
questions.e: E. & O.E. stands for "errors and omissions excepted": the seller keeps the right to correct mistakes found in the invoice after it is sent. It says nothing about risk or expenses.

questions.s: A trade discount is allowed by a seller
o: only when the buyer pays before the due date
by the bank on early payment of a bill
on the list price, usually to traders buying for resale
only after the buyer has returned faulty goods and received a credit note
questions.e: Trade discount is a reduction on the catalogue or list price given to traders, often for bulk buying, and is deducted on the invoice itself. A reduction for paying early is a cash discount.

questions.s: Goods listed at Rs. 40,000 are sold with 10 % trade discount and 5 % cash discount for payment within 10 days. If the buyer pays within 10 days, he pays
questions.e: Trade discount first: 40,000 − 4,000 = 36,000. Cash discount on that: 5 % of 36,000 = 1,800, leaving 34,200. Taking 15 % of 40,000 at once gives 34,000, but the cash discount is calculated on the price after trade discount.

questions.s: Under an F.O.B. (free on board) contract, the seller bears the costs of the goods
o: including marine insurance up to the port of destination
until they reach the buyer's own warehouse in the importing country
only until they leave the seller's factory gate
until they are loaded on the ship at the port of shipment
questions.e: In an F.O.B. price, the exporter pays all charges up to loading the goods on board; freight and insurance beyond that are the buyer's. Including insurance and freight to the destination port describes a C.I.F. price.

questions.s: A C.I.F. price quoted by a Karachi exporter includes
o: the cost of goods, insurance and freight to the port of destination
the cost of goods and inland carriage to Karachi port
the cost of goods only, at the exporter's factory
the cost of goods and the customs duty paid by the importer in his own country
questions.e: C.I.F. means cost, insurance and freight: the exporter's price covers the goods plus their insurance and sea freight to the buyer's port. Import duty in the buyer's country is paid by the importer and is not part of C.I.F.

questions.s: A price that includes all expenses up to the buyer's own premises is called a
questions.e: A franco price covers every cost of delivering goods to the buyer's door. A loco price is the opposite: the price at the seller's premises, with all carriage paid by the buyer.

questions.s: The document issued by a shipping company acknowledging receipt of goods on board and acting as a document of title is the
questions.e: The bill of lading is the shipowner's receipt, the evidence of the contract of carriage and a document of title that can be transferred by endorsement. A mate's receipt is only a temporary receipt given at loading and later exchanged for the bill of lading.

questions.s: A mate's receipt is
o: a contract for hiring a whole ship for a voyage
the final document of title that the importer presents at the destination
a certificate issued by a chamber of commerce stating the country where goods were made
issued by the ship's officer on loading and later exchanged for a bill of lading
questions.e: The mate (an officer of the ship) signs a receipt as goods are loaded; the exporter hands it to the shipping company to obtain the bill of lading. It is not itself the final document of title.

questions.s: A document that certifies the country in which exported goods were produced is a
questions.e: A certificate of origin, commonly issued by a chamber of commerce, proves where goods were made so that the importing country can apply the correct duty. A bill of entry is the importer's declaration to customs, not proof of origin.

questions.s: A letter of credit is mainly used in foreign trade because it
o: replaces the need for marine insurance on the cargo
assures the exporter that a bank will pay once the agreed documents are presented
gives the importer full legal ownership of the goods while they are still at sea on the ship
allows the exporter to avoid preparing any shipping documents
questions.e: Under a letter of credit, the importer's bank undertakes to pay the exporter against specified documents such as the bill of lading and invoice, removing doubt about payment. It does not transfer ownership of goods; the bill of lading does that.

questions.s: An indent in foreign trade is
o: a permit issued by customs to release goods
a receipt issued by a warehouse for imported goods
an order placed by an importer with an agent to import goods for him
a list of all the goods sent by the exporter on the ship, prepared by its captain
questions.e: An indent is an order sent through an indent house or agent who arranges the import on the importer's behalf. A list of goods sent with the ship is the ship's manifest, not an indent.

questions.s: In a closed indent, the importer
o: buys goods from the local wholesale market
names the particular manufacturer from whom the goods must be bought
pays the agent only after the imported goods have all been sold in the local market
leaves the choice of supplier entirely to the agent
questions.e: A closed (specific) indent names the manufacturer, so the agent has no choice of supplier. An open indent leaves the choice of manufacturer to the agent.

questions.s: Before goods can be cleared from customs, an importer submits a statement of their description, quantity and value to the customs authorities. This document is the
questions.e: The importer's declaration to customs for clearing imported goods is the bill of entry. The shipping bill is the matching document prepared by an exporter for goods leaving the country.

questions.s: A consular invoice is
o: a pro forma invoice prepared for a government tender
an invoice prepared by the customs office at the port of arrival
a bill sent by the shipping company for sea freight
an invoice certified by the importing country's consul in the exporting country
questions.e: Some importing countries require the invoice to be certified by their consul stationed in the exporter's country, to check value and prevent false declarations. It is not a customs or freight document.

questions.s: A dock warrant is
o: a receipt given by the mate on loading cargo
a fine imposed for late removal of goods
a permit allowing a ship to enter the harbour
a document of title for goods stored in a dock warehouse
questions.e: Dock authorities issue a dock warrant for goods kept in their warehouse; it can be transferred by endorsement, so the goods can be sold without moving them. The receipt given at loading is the mate's receipt.

questions.s: Barter means
o: exchanging goods directly for goods without using money
buying goods on credit for later payment
exchanging money of one country for another
questions.e: Under barter, a farmer might exchange wheat for cloth with no money involved. Exchanging one currency for another is foreign exchange, not barter.

questions.s: The main difficulty of the barter system was the
o: very high rates of interest charged on all loans
lack of double coincidence of wants
questions.e: Barter works only if each party wants exactly what the other offers, at the same time and in suitable amounts, which is rare. Money solved this by acting as a common medium of exchange.

questions.s: Mining, fishing and quarrying are examples of
questions.e: Extractive industries take wealth directly from the land, water or air. Genetic industries instead breed and rear plants or animals, as in poultry farms and nurseries.

questions.s: A poultry farm that rears chicks for sale is an example of a
questions.e: Genetic industries reproduce and multiply living things, such as poultry, cattle breeding and plant nurseries. Extractive industries remove natural resources without breeding them.

questions.s: Converting cotton into yarn and cloth in a Faisalabad mill is an example of
questions.e: Manufacturing changes raw materials into finished or semi-finished goods with a higher value. Commerce only distributes goods once they are made.

questions.s: A broker differs from a factor in that a broker
o: keeps the goods and sells them in his own name
guarantees payment by the buyers for an extra commission
brings buyer and seller together without taking possession of the goods
buys the goods outright and resells them at a profit
questions.e: A broker is a go-between who arranges contracts but does not hold the goods. A factor has possession of the goods and can sell them in his own name.

questions.s: An agent who, for an extra commission, guarantees his principal against bad debts from the buyers he finds is a
questions.e: A del credere agent takes on the risk of buyers not paying and is paid an extra (del credere) commission for this guarantee. An ordinary broker gives no such guarantee.

questions.s: Under the balance of trade, a country has a deficit when
o: its banks lend more than they hold in deposits
its exports of goods exceed its imports of goods
its government spends more than it collects in taxes
its imports of goods exceed its exports of goods
questions.e: The balance of trade compares visible exports and imports. An excess of imports over exports is a deficit; spending more than tax revenue is a budget deficit, a different idea.

questions.s: The balance of payments differs from the balance of trade because it
o: records only trade with neighbouring countries
includes only the exports and imports of goods
includes services, transfers and capital flows as well as goods
is prepared by commercial banks for their clients
questions.e: The balance of trade covers goods only. The balance of payments records all transactions with the rest of the world, including services, remittances and capital movements.

questions.s: Sialkot is widely known for exporting
o: crude oil, natural gas and petroleum products
questions.e: Sialkot's small and medium industries have long made footballs, other sports goods and surgical instruments for export. Rock salt comes mainly from the Salt Range, not Sialkot.

questions.s: Which factor most strongly influences the location of an industry that uses a heavy, bulky raw material which loses much of its weight in processing?
o: nearness to the source of the raw material
questions.e: If a raw material loses weight in processing, carrying it far is wasteful, so such industries, for example sugar mills near cane fields, locate close to the raw material. Nearness to consumers matters more for goods that gain weight or are perishable after manufacture.

questions.s: Gwadar port is located in the province of
questions.e: Gwadar is on the Makran coast of Balochistan. Pakistan's other major ports, Karachi Port and Port Qasim, are both in Sindh.

questions.s: A commission agent is paid
o: interest on the money he lends to buyers
a percentage of the value of the business he arranges
the whole profit made on goods he sells
a fixed monthly salary regardless of sales
questions.e: A commission agent works for a principal and receives commission, a percentage of the sales or purchases he makes. Keeping the whole profit is what a merchant who buys on his own account does.

questions.s: A large retail shop that sells only one kind of product, such as shoes, in many styles and sizes is a
questions.e: A single-line store concentrates on one line of goods and offers wide choice within it. A departmental or general store sells many unrelated lines.

questions.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the aids to trade?
questions.e: Banking, warehousing, advertising, insurance and transport help trade take place, so they are aids to trade. Manufacturing is part of industry: it makes the goods that trade then distributes.

questions.s: Selling goods to buyers in other countries is called
questions.e: Export trade sends home-produced goods to foreign buyers. Import trade is buying goods from abroad.

questions.s: The main function of banking as an aid to trade is to remove the hindrance of
questions.e: Banks provide loans, overdrafts and means of payment, solving the trader's shortage of funds. The hindrance of place is removed by transport.

questions.s: A retailer who sells from a small shop in a residential street, often giving credit to known customers, is a
questions.e: A local general store stocks daily necessities near customers' homes and often gives credit to regular buyers. A hawker has no fixed shop.

questions.s: The term "cash on delivery" means that
o: the buyer pays when the goods are handed over to him
the seller pays the carrier's charges in full
the buyer pays in advance before the goods are sent
the buyer pays three months after receiving the goods and the invoice
questions.e: With cash on delivery, payment is collected when the goods are delivered. Paying before goods are sent is payment in advance.

questions.s: Goods listed at Rs. 80,000 carry trade discounts of 10 % and then a further 5 %. What is the invoice price?
questions.e: Successive discounts are applied one after another: 80,000 × 0.90 = 72,000, then 72,000 × 0.95 = 68,400. Adding them to 15 % gives 68,000, which is wrong because the second discount is taken on the reduced price.

questions.s: A delivery note is sent
o: by a bank, confirming payment to the seller
by customs, allowing goods to leave the port
before the order, quoting prices and terms
with the goods, listing what has been delivered
questions.e: A delivery note travels with the goods; the buyer checks and signs it as proof of receipt. Prices and terms before an order appear in a quotation.

questions.s: Goods sent by air are accompanied by a receipt and contract of carriage called the
questions.e: The airline or its agent issues an airway bill as a receipt and evidence of the contract of carriage; unlike a bill of lading, it is normally not a document of title. A bill of lading is used for goods sent by sea.

questions.s: An importer pays an indent house to arrange imports. The indent house earns
o: interest on the importer's bank deposit
a commission on the value of goods imported
the customs duty paid on the goods
questions.e: An indent house acts as agent and is rewarded by commission. Customs duty goes to the government and freight to the carrier.

questions.s: An auctioneer sells goods by
o: keeping goods on display in a chain of shops
quoting a fixed price that cannot change
inviting bids in public and selling to the highest bidder
questions.e: At an auction, buyers bid against each other and the goods go to the highest bid. A fixed, non-negotiable price is a one-price shop's method.

questions.s: In an open indent, the agent
o: is free to buy from any suitable manufacturer
sells the importer's goods in a foreign market
pays customs duty on behalf of the exporter
must buy from the manufacturer named by the importer
questions.e: An open indent states the goods, price limits and terms but leaves the choice of supplier to the agent. Naming the supplier makes it a closed indent.

questions.s: Which aid to trade brings buyers' attention to new products?
questions.e: Advertising informs and persuades buyers about goods and services. Insurance only covers risks of loss.

questions.s: A Lahore firm imports machinery from China and sells it to a buyer in Afghanistan without using it. This is an example of
questions.e: Goods brought into a country and sent on to a third country are re-exported, which is entrepot trade. It is not simple export trade, because the machinery was not produced in Pakistan.

questions.s: A shopkeeper in Multan does not know that a new brand of ceiling fan exists in the market. The aid to trade that removes this hindrance is
questions.e: Lack of information about goods is the hindrance of knowledge, which advertising removes by telling buyers what is available. Banking removes the hindrance of finance, not of information.

questions.s: A contract under which a trader hires a whole ship, or a large part of it, for a voyage or a period is a
questions.e: A charter party is the agreement for hiring a ship. A bill of lading is used when goods are sent as ordinary cargo on a ship that also carries other shippers' goods.

questions.s: Commercial activity in Pakistan is most concentrated in Karachi chiefly because it
o: is the country's main seaport and industrial centre
lies at the centre of the Punjab plain
is close to the main coal mines of the country
is the federal capital of the country
questions.e: Karachi's seaports handle most of Pakistan's foreign trade, and industry, banks and offices cluster around them. The federal capital is Islamabad, not Karachi.

questions.s: A business owned and controlled by one person, who takes all the profit and bears all the risk, is a
o: partnership firm formed by one family
questions.e: In a sole proprietorship one person supplies the capital, manages the business and keeps all the profit or loss. A partnership needs at least two persons, even if they belong to one family.

questions.s: The liability of a sole proprietor for the debts of his business is
o: unlimited, so his private property can be used to pay them
limited to the value of the shop, its fittings and the stock held in it
shared equally with the business's creditors
limited to the capital he has put into the business
questions.e: The law does not separate a sole trader from his business, so creditors can claim his personal assets if business assets are not enough. Liability limited to capital invested is a feature of shareholders in a limited company.

questions.s: Which of the following is a main advantage of a sole proprietorship?
o: quick decisions and close personal contact with customers
an unlimited supply of capital from the general public
a legal existence that continues after the owner's death
liability of the owner limited to the amount he has invested in the shop
questions.e: A sole trader can decide at once without consulting anyone and knows his customers personally. Perpetual existence and limited liability belong to companies, and a sole trader cannot raise capital from the public.

questions.s: A major limitation of a sole proprietorship is
o: the need to share profits among many owners
limited capital and managing ability of one person
strict legal formalities and registration with the SECP for setting it up
the requirement to publish annual accounts
questions.e: One person can raise only so much money and has limited time and skills, which restricts growth. A sole trader keeps all the profit, so profit sharing is not a limitation, and very few formalities are needed to start.

questions.s: The law governing partnership firms in Pakistan is the
questions.e: Partnerships in Pakistan are governed by the Partnership Act, 1932, inherited from the subcontinent's pre-independence law. The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 deals with cheques, bills and notes.

questions.s: The minimum number of persons needed to form a partnership is
questions.e: A partnership is a relation between persons who agree to share the profits of a business, so at least two persons are needed. A single owner forms a sole proprietorship.

questions.s: The written agreement that sets out the terms of a partnership, such as capital, profit-sharing ratio and duties, is the
questions.e: Partners record their terms in a partnership deed. The memorandum and articles of association are documents of a company, and a prospectus invites the public to buy a company's shares.

questions.s: If the partnership deed is silent on the matter, profits and losses are shared among the partners
o: only by the active partners and not the others
in the ratio of the capital each partner contributed
in proportion to the hours each partner works
questions.e: Under partnership law, when there is no agreement, partners share profits and losses equally. Sharing in the capital ratio is a common mistake: it applies only if the partners have agreed to it.

questions.s: A partner who contributes capital and shares profits but takes no part in running the business is a
questions.e: A sleeping (dormant) partner invests and shares profits but does not take part in management; he is still liable to outsiders like other partners. A nominal partner lends only his name and usually invests no capital.

questions.s: A well-known person who allows his name to be used by a firm, but invests no capital and takes no share of profit, is a
questions.e: A nominal partner lends his name and reputation only. A sleeping partner, by contrast, invests capital and shares profits.

questions.s: Under the Partnership Act, 1932, a minor
o: can be admitted to the benefits of partnership with the consent of all partners
can never receive any share in the profits of a firm
can become a full partner with unlimited personal liability
must be appointed as the managing partner of the firm by the other partners at once
questions.e: A minor cannot enter into a contract, so he cannot be a full partner; with all partners' consent he may be admitted to the benefits of partnership, and his liability is limited to his share in the firm. He has no personal liability for the firm's debts while a minor.

questions.s: Under the Partnership Act, 1932, registration of a firm is
o: required only for firms with more than ten partners
optional, but an unregistered firm cannot sue third parties to enforce contracts
possible only after the firm has made its first profit
compulsory before the firm can begin any business at all
questions.e: The Act does not make registration compulsory, but an unregistered firm and its partners lose the right to sue outsiders on the firm's contracts. It is not true that an unregistered firm cannot do business at all.

questions.s: "Mutual agency" in a partnership means that
o: each partner is an agent of the firm and of the other partners
partners must appoint an outside agent to manage the firm
the firm acts as a commission agent for other businesses in the same trade
a partner can act only after all others agree in writing
questions.e: Every partner can bind the firm and the other partners by acts done in the ordinary course of business, and is bound by their acts too. This is why partners must trust one another.

questions.s: A partnership with no fixed period, which any partner can end by giving notice, is a
questions.e: When the deed sets no time limit, the partnership is "at will" and may be dissolved by notice from any partner. A particular partnership is formed for one venture or a fixed period.

questions.s: The liability of partners in an ordinary partnership firm is
o: limited to the capital each partner contributed
borne only by the partner who caused the debt
limited to the amount stated in the partnership deed
questions.e: Each partner is liable for all the firm's debts, both together and individually, so a creditor can recover the whole amount from any one partner. Limited liability is a company feature.

questions.s: A partnership firm is compulsorily dissolved when
o: the firm suffers a loss in one year
all partners, or all but one, are declared insolvent
one partner goes on a long trip abroad
a new partner is admitted to the firm with the consent of every existing partner
questions.e: Compulsory dissolution happens when continuing becomes impossible or unlawful, such as the insolvency of all or all but one partner, or the business becoming illegal. A loss in one year or admitting a partner does not end the firm.

questions.s: A joint stock company is
o: an informal association that needs no registration
a group of partners who share unlimited liability
a business owned by one person with limited liability
an artificial person created by law with a separate legal entity
questions.e: A company is formed by registration under the companies law and becomes a legal person separate from its members; it can own property and sue in its own name. Unlimited liability belongs to ordinary partnerships.

questions.s: "Perpetual succession" of a company means that
o: the eldest son of a director automatically becomes a director when his father dies
profits are kept forever and never paid as dividends
the company continues to exist even if its members change or die
the company's shares can never be sold to outsiders
questions.e: Because the company is a separate legal person, its life does not depend on its members; shares change hands and the company continues. It has nothing to do with inheriting directorships.

questions.s: In Pakistan, companies are registered with, and regulated by, the
o: Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan
questions.e: The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) registers companies through its company registry and regulates them. The State Bank regulates banks, and the stock exchange is a market for securities, not a registrar.

questions.s: The liability of a shareholder in a company limited by shares is
o: fixed by the directors after each loss
limited to the unpaid amount, if any, on the shares he holds
equal to the total debts of the company
unlimited, like that of a partner in an ordinary partnership firm under the 1932 Act
questions.e: A shareholder can be asked to pay only what remains unpaid on his shares; once they are fully paid, he owes nothing more for the company's debts. Unlimited liability is the position of partners.

questions.s: The articles of association of a company mainly contain
o: an invitation to the public to buy shares
the objects for which the company is formed
the certificate that brings the company into being
rules for the internal management of the company
questions.e: Articles deal with matters such as meetings, voting, the appointment of directors and transfer of shares. The objects are set out in the memorandum.

questions.s: A company comes into existence as a legal person on the date shown on its
questions.e: On registration, the registrar issues a certificate of incorporation, and from that date the company is a legal entity. A prospectus is issued later, if the company invites the public to buy shares.

questions.s: A prospectus is issued by a public company to
o: lay down the rules for meetings of directors
record the minutes of the annual general meeting of shareholders for the registrar
invite the public to subscribe for its shares or debentures
prove that the company has been registered
questions.e: A prospectus gives details of the company and the securities offered so that the public can decide whether to invest. Rules for meetings appear in the articles.

questions.s: The doctrine of constructive notice means that anyone dealing with a company is
o: required to inspect the company's accounts before dealing
presumed to know the contents of its memorandum and articles
protected against all acts of the directors
entitled to assume that internal rules have been followed
questions.e: Because the memorandum and articles are public documents, outsiders are treated as knowing what they contain. The right to assume internal procedures were followed is the separate doctrine of indoor management.

questions.s: A supplier dealing in good faith with a company is entitled to assume that its internal procedures, such as passing a needed resolution, have been properly followed. This is the doctrine of
questions.e: The doctrine of indoor management protects outsiders who cannot see into the company's internal affairs. Constructive notice works the other way, presuming outsiders know the public documents.

questions.s: Persons who conceive the idea of a company and take the steps needed to form it are called
questions.e: Promoters find the business opportunity, arrange the capital and prepare documents for registration. Directors are appointed to manage the company once it exists.

questions.s: A key difference between a private and a public company is that a private company
o: does not need to be registered under the companies law
must have at least seven directors on its board and publish a prospectus each year
cannot invite the general public to subscribe for its shares
has unlimited liability for all its members
questions.e: A private company restricts the transfer of its shares and is not allowed to offer them to the public; a public company can issue a prospectus. Both are registered and both can have limited liability.

questions.s: The holders of ordinary shares in a company are
o: its bankers, entitled to repayment on demand
its owners, with voting rights and a varying dividend
its employees, entitled to a fixed monthly wage
its creditors, entitled to fixed interest every year
questions.e: Ordinary shareholders own the company, vote at meetings and receive whatever dividend the directors declare from profits. Creditors who earn fixed interest are debenture holders.

questions.s: Preference shareholders have priority over ordinary shareholders in
o: voting at every general meeting of the company
receiving all of the profit that is left after paying expenses and taxes each year
payment of a fixed dividend and return of capital on winding up
electing the board of directors each year
questions.e: Preference shares carry a fixed rate of dividend that is paid before any ordinary dividend, and capital is repaid to them first on winding up. They usually do not have normal voting rights.

questions.s: For cumulative preference shares, a dividend not paid in a loss-making year
o: is carried forward and paid in a later year before ordinary dividends
lapses and is never paid to the shareholders
is paid by the directors from their own pockets
is converted into ordinary shares at once
questions.e: With cumulative preference shares, unpaid dividends accumulate as arrears that must be cleared before ordinary shareholders receive anything. For non-cumulative preference shares, the unpaid dividend lapses.

questions.s: A debenture holder of a company is
o: an owner of the company who shares in its profits through dividends each year
a member who votes at the annual general meeting
a creditor who lends money and receives a fixed rate of interest
a director who receives a monthly fee
questions.e: A debenture is an acknowledgement of a loan to the company; its holder earns interest whether or not the company makes a profit. Shareholders, not debenture holders, own the company and receive dividends.

questions.s: Shares issued free of charge to existing shareholders out of a company's accumulated profits are called
questions.e: Bonus shares capitalise reserves: shareholders receive extra shares without paying for them. Right shares are offered to existing shareholders but must be paid for.

questions.s: When a company offers new shares first to its existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings, it is making a
questions.e: A right issue protects existing shareholders' proportion of ownership, and they pay for the new shares. A bonus issue is free, and a public issue is offered to everyone through a prospectus.

questions.s: The maximum amount of capital a company is allowed to raise by issuing shares, as stated in its memorandum, is its
questions.e: Authorised (nominal) capital is the upper limit fixed in the memorandum. Issued capital is the part actually offered to investors, which can be equal to or less than the authorised capital.

questions.s: A company has issued 100,000 shares of Rs. 10 each and has called Rs. 8 per share. All calls have been received except Rs. 2 per share on 5,000 shares. Its paid-up capital is
questions.e: Called-up capital is 100,000 × Rs. 8 = Rs. 800,000. Calls in arrears are 5,000 × Rs. 2 = Rs. 10,000, so paid-up capital is Rs. 790,000. Rs. 800,000 is the called-up amount, before deducting the unpaid calls.

questions.s: When a company issues a share of face value Rs. 10 for Rs. 12, the extra Rs. 2 is called
questions.e: Issuing shares above face value is an issue at a premium; the extra amount goes to a share premium account. A dividend is a share of profit paid to shareholders, not an amount paid by them.

questions.s: Part of the uncalled capital that a company decides by special resolution will be called only if the company is wound up is
questions.e: Reserve capital is kept back as a safety margin for creditors and can be called only on winding up. Working capital is an accounting idea (current assets less current liabilities), not a class of share capital.

questions.s: If a shareholder fails to pay a call on his shares after due notice, the company may, if its articles allow,
o: transfer them to a director free
questions.e: Forfeiture cancels the shares of a member who fails to pay calls, and the amount already paid is usually lost to him. It must follow the procedure in the articles, including a proper notice.

questions.s: A resolution passed by a simple majority of votes at a general meeting is an
questions.e: An ordinary resolution needs more votes in favour than against. A special resolution needs a larger majority of at least three-fourths of the votes cast.

questions.s: A special resolution of a company requires
o: the approval of the board of directors only
the written consent of every single member of the company, including absent members
a simple majority of the members present at the meeting
at least three-fourths of the votes cast by members present and voting
questions.e: Special resolutions are needed for major decisions, such as altering the articles, and require a three-fourths majority of votes cast. A simple majority is enough only for an ordinary resolution.

questions.s: The minimum number of members who must be present for a meeting to transact business validly is the
questions.e: Without a quorum, decisions taken at a meeting are invalid. The agenda is the list of business, and minutes are the written record of what was decided.

questions.s: A person appointed by a shareholder to attend and vote at a general meeting on his behalf is a
questions.e: A member who cannot attend may appoint a proxy to vote for him. A promoter takes part in forming the company, not in voting for members.

questions.s: The annual general meeting of a company is held mainly to
o: prepare the prospectus for a new public issue
settle disputes among partners of the firm
consider the accounts, declare dividends and elect directors
register the company and receive its certificate
questions.e: At the AGM, shareholders receive the audited accounts and directors' report, approve dividends, and elect directors and auditors. Registration happens before the company exists, long before any AGM.

questions.s: A cooperative society is mainly formed to
o: trade in shares on the stock exchange
serve its members rather than to earn maximum profit
carry out government policy as a public enterprise
earn the highest possible profit for a few investors
questions.e: A cooperative's chief aim is service: members pool resources to buy, sell or borrow on better terms for themselves. Profit maximisation is the usual aim of companies.

questions.s: Voting in a cooperative society is based on the principle of
o: one member, one vote, whatever the shares held
votes in proportion to the purchases each member made during the year
one share, one vote, as in a company
votes given only to founding members
questions.e: Cooperatives are run democratically: each member has one vote, however much capital he has put in. One share, one vote is the company rule.

questions.s: A society formed by consumers to buy goods in bulk and sell them to members at fair prices is a
questions.e: A consumers' cooperative cuts out middlemen to supply members with daily goods. A producers' cooperative is formed by small producers to buy raw materials and sell their output.

questions.s: Farmers in a village join together to borrow money at low interest for seeds and fertiliser. They have formed a
questions.e: A credit cooperative collects savings and lends to members at reasonable interest, saving them from moneylenders. A marketing cooperative instead helps members sell their produce.

questions.s: In a cooperative society, surplus that remains after paying a limited dividend on capital is usually distributed
o: to the government as a special tax on the income of all cooperative societies
entirely to the managing committee as a bonus
among members strictly in proportion to the shares they hold
among members in proportion to the business they did with the society
questions.e: The patronage bonus rewards members according to their purchases or sales through the society, which reflects the service motive. Dividing all surplus by capital would be the company principle.

questions.s: A business owned and controlled by the government is called a
questions.e: Public enterprises are owned, financed and controlled by the state, at the federal or provincial level. Private companies and sole proprietorships are owned by private individuals.

questions.s: A public enterprise run directly by a government ministry, financed through the government budget and staffed by civil servants, is a
questions.e: A departmental undertaking, such as a railway run by a ministry, is part of the government itself. A statutory corporation is created by a special Act and has its own legal identity.

questions.s: A public corporation differs from a departmental undertaking mainly because the corporation
o: is managed directly by a ministry's civil servants
is owned by private shareholders who elect its directors at the annual general meeting
is financed only through the annual federal budget
is created by a special Act and has a separate legal entity
questions.e: A statutory (public) corporation is set up by its own Act of the legislature, can own property and sue in its own name, and enjoys more operational freedom. Budget finance and ministry control describe a departmental undertaking.

questions.s: A company in which the government holds at least a majority of the share capital is a
questions.e: A government company is registered under the companies law like any other company, but the state owns the majority of its shares. A departmental undertaking is not a company at all.

questions.s: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a joint stock company?
o: separate legal entity from its members
mutual agency among all its members
transferability of shares in a public company
questions.e: In a company, members are not agents of one another; the company acts through its directors. Mutual agency is a feature of partnership, where each partner can bind the others.

questions.s: The owner of a sole proprietorship keeps
o: a share decided by his creditors
all the profit of the business
only a salary fixed by law
half the profit, the rest going to the state
questions.e: The sole proprietor bears all the risk and so is entitled to all the profit. Sharing profit is a feature of partnership.

questions.s: A partner who is not known to the public as a partner but takes an active part in the business is a
questions.e: A secret partner manages the business but his partnership is hidden from outsiders. A nominal partner is the opposite: publicly known but with no real role.

questions.s: Admitting a new partner to an existing firm generally requires
o: the consent of all the existing partners
the consent of the senior partner only
the approval of the registrar of firms
questions.e: Because partnership rests on mutual trust and agency, no person can be introduced as a partner without the consent of all partners, unless the deed provides otherwise. Special resolutions belong to companies.

questions.s: A company's relations with outsiders and its permitted activities are set out in its
questions.e: The memorandum states the company's objects and powers, which outsiders deal with. The articles concern internal management.

questions.s: Dividends on ordinary shares are
o: paid every year whether or not there is a profit
fixed in advance at the time the shares are issued
paid before the preference dividend, as ordinary shares carry the first right to profit
paid out of profits at a rate recommended by the directors
questions.e: Ordinary dividends vary with profit and are paid only after the preference dividend. A fixed rate in advance is a feature of preference shares.

questions.s: Interest on debentures must be paid
o: only if the company makes a profit that year
even if the company makes a loss in that year
only after all the dividends to shareholders have been declared and paid
only when shareholders vote to pay it
questions.e: Debenture interest is a charge on the company, owed to creditors regardless of profit. Dividends, by contrast, depend on profits.

questions.s: Debentures that are secured by a charge on the company's assets are called
questions.e: Secured (mortgage) debentures give holders a claim on specified assets if the company fails to pay. Naked debentures carry no such security.

questions.s: Preference shares that the company can buy back after a fixed period or at its option are called
questions.e: Redeemable preference shares are repaid by the company under the terms of issue. Convertible preference shares are instead changed into ordinary shares.

questions.s: A cooperative society is managed by
o: a board appointed by the State Bank
the member with the largest share capital
a committee elected by its members
the government officer who registered it
questions.e: Democratic management is a basic cooperative principle: members elect a managing committee. Control by the largest investor would contradict one member, one vote.

questions.s: Which form of business is most suitable for a small grocery shop in a town?
questions.e: A small shop needs little capital and gains from quick decisions and personal service, which suits a sole proprietor. Public companies and corporations are for large-scale undertakings.

questions.s: A company that controls another company by holding more than half of its voting shares is a
questions.e: The controlling company is the holding company; the one controlled is its subsidiary. A cooperative is a different form of organisation altogether.

questions.s: A sleeping partner is liable to the firm's creditors
o: only up to the profits he has received
fully, in the same way as the active partners
only if he is also a nominal partner
not at all, since he takes no part in management
questions.e: Not taking part in management does not reduce a partner's liability: a sleeping partner is liable without limit for the firm's debts. Only a minor admitted to benefits has limited liability.

questions.s: The document that defines a company's name, registered office, objects and the liability of its members is the
questions.e: The memorandum is the company's charter; it states what the company is and what it can do, and it governs its relations with outsiders. The articles contain internal rules of management.

questions.s: Under the doctrine of ultra vires, an act of a company that is beyond the objects in its memorandum is
o: valid if it earns a profit for the company
void, and cannot be made valid even if all members approve it
valid, provided the directors approve it at a board meeting
voidable at the choice of the company's creditors
questions.e: An act outside the memorandum's objects is beyond the company's legal powers and is void from the start; even unanimous approval by shareholders cannot ratify it. Approval by directors or the profit earned makes no difference.

questions.s: The two primary functions of a commercial bank are
o: buying shares and running insurance policies for depositors
providing lockers and collecting utility bills for customers
issuing currency notes and controlling credit in the economy
questions.e: A commercial bank's basic business is to take deposits from the public and lend them out. Issuing notes and controlling credit are functions of the central bank.

questions.s: A bank account mainly used by traders, with no limit on the number of withdrawals by cheque, is a
o: savings account with a monthly limit
questions.e: A current account suits businesses that make many payments; withdrawals by cheque are allowed any number of times, and usually no profit or interest is paid. Fixed deposits cannot be withdrawn freely before maturity.

questions.s: Money deposited in a bank for a fixed period, which earns a higher return and cannot normally be withdrawn before that period ends, is a
questions.e: A fixed (term) deposit locks the money for an agreed period in return for a higher rate. Current deposits are payable on demand and are also called demand deposits.

questions.s: An overdraft is a facility that allows a customer to
o: withdraw his fixed deposit before its maturity date at no cost
draw more than the balance in his current account, up to a limit
deposit money at a branch in another city without paying any charges at all
borrow against gold kept in his locker at any other bank
questions.e: With an overdraft, the bank lets a current-account holder overdraw up to an agreed limit, charging only on the amount actually used. Breaking a fixed deposit early is not an overdraft.

questions.s: Which of the following is an agency service of a bank?
o: providing safe deposit lockers to the public for rent
issuing letters of credit for importers and travellers
collecting cheques and dividends on behalf of customers
accepting fixed deposits from members of the public
questions.e: In agency services, the bank acts as its customer's agent, for example collecting cheques, paying bills on standing instructions or buying shares for him. Lockers and letters of credit are general utility services.

questions.s: A bank's safe deposit lockers, travellers' cheques and letters of credit are examples of its
questions.e: General utility services are offered to customers and the public without the bank acting as anyone's agent. Agency services are those performed on the customer's behalf, such as collecting cheques.

questions.s: Which institution acts as the banker to the Government of Pakistan and controls the issue of currency notes?
questions.e: The State Bank of Pakistan is the central bank; it issues currency notes, regulates other banks and manages monetary policy. The National Bank of Pakistan is a commercial bank, though owned largely by the government.

questions.s: The State Bank of Pakistan was established in
questions.e: The State Bank of Pakistan began working on 1 July 1948 and was inaugurated by Quaid-e-Azam. Pakistan came into being in 1947, but the Reserve Bank of India continued as the central bank until mid-1948.

questions.s: The central bank is called the "lender of last resort" because it
o: gives loans to the public only after all banks refuse them
is the last bank in the country to open its doors to customers each working day
lends to the government at the end of each financial year
lends to commercial banks when they cannot get funds elsewhere
questions.e: When banks face a cash shortage that no one else will meet, the central bank provides funds to prevent a banking crisis. It does not lend directly to the public in this role.

questions.s: Which of the following is a function of the State Bank of Pakistan and not of a commercial bank?
questions.e: The sole right to issue currency notes belongs to the central bank. Deposits, overdrafts and collection of cheques are ordinary commercial banking services.

questions.s: When the central bank buys government securities in the open market, the effect is to
o: increase the cash with commercial banks and expand credit
raise the cash reserve ratio that banks must maintain
stop banks from accepting new deposits for some time
reduce the cash with commercial banks and contract credit
questions.e: In open market operations, buying securities pays money into the banking system, so banks can lend more. Selling securities does the reverse and contracts credit.

questions.s: To reduce credit in the economy, the central bank is most likely to
o: allow banks to keep smaller cash reserves
buy government securities from commercial banks
raise the cash reserve ratio banks must keep with it
lower its policy rate for lending to banks
questions.e: A higher cash reserve ratio leaves banks less money to lend, so credit contracts. Buying securities and lowering the policy rate both expand credit.

questions.s: Under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a promissory note is
o: a receipt issued by a bank to a customer for a fixed deposit of money for one year
an unconditional written order by the drawer to the drawee to pay
an unconditional written promise by the maker to pay a certain sum
a written order on a banker that is payable on demand only
questions.e: A promissory note contains a promise to pay, signed by the maker, and has two parties: maker and payee. An order to pay is the essence of a bill of exchange.

questions.s: The number of parties in a bill of exchange is ordinarily
o: four: drawer, drawee, payee and banker
questions.e: A bill of exchange is an order by the drawer on the drawee to pay the payee. A promissory note has only two parties, the maker and the payee.

questions.s: A cheque is a bill of exchange that is
o: a promise by a bank to pay the holder on demand
drawn on any person and payable after three months
payable only after acceptance by the drawee
drawn on a specified banker and payable on demand
questions.e: Under the 1881 Act, a cheque is a bill drawn on a specified banker and always payable on demand. Unlike a time bill, it does not need acceptance.

questions.s: Under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a bill payable three months after date is entitled to
o: seven days of grace added to the due date
no days of grace, as it is a time bill
three days of grace added to the due date
thirty days of grace after presentation
questions.e: A bill or note payable otherwise than on demand gets three days of grace, so its maturity is three days after the due date. Instruments payable on demand, such as cheques, get no days of grace.

questions.s: A bill dated 10 January is payable two months after date. Allowing days of grace, its date of maturity is
questions.e: Two months after 10 January is 10 March; adding three days of grace gives 13 March. 10 March forgets the days of grace.

questions.s: The person to whom a bill of exchange is addressed and who is asked to pay it is the
questions.e: The drawer writes the order, the drawee is directed to pay, and the payee receives payment. When the drawee accepts the bill he is called the acceptor.

questions.s: A cheque is crossed generally by
o: drawing two parallel transverse lines across its face
signing it on the back before handing it over
writing the word "bearer" clearly after the payee's name on the cheque
writing the name of a bank between two lines
questions.e: General crossing is two parallel lines across the cheque, with or without words such as "& Co.". Writing a bank's name between the lines makes it a special crossing.

questions.s: A generally crossed cheque
o: becomes payable only after three days of grace have passed from its date of issue
can be cashed at the counter by any person who holds it
cannot be cashed at the counter and must be paid through a bank account
can be paid only to the bank named between the crossing lines
questions.e: Crossing is a safeguard: the money must go into a bank account, so the person receiving it can be traced. Payment only to a named bank applies to a special crossing.

questions.s: When the name of a particular bank is written between the crossing lines, the paying banker
o: must return it unpaid to the drawer
pays the cheque only through that named bank
may pay it through any bank the holder chooses
pays it in cash to the holder at the counter
questions.e: A special crossing restricts payment to the bank named in the crossing. Payment through any bank is the effect of a general crossing.

questions.s: The words "Not Negotiable" written within the crossing of a cheque mean that
o: the cheque is valid only for three days after its date
a transferee gets no better title than the person who transferred it
the cheque cannot be transferred to anyone at all
the cheque can be paid only in cash at the counter
questions.e: A "Not Negotiable" crossing does not stop transfer; it removes the special protection of negotiability, so a person taking it from a thief gets no good title. The common mistake is to think it cannot be transferred at all.

questions.s: An "Account Payee" crossing directs the collecting banker to
o: credit the amount only to the account of the payee named
pay the amount in cash to the payee at the counter
credit the account of whoever presents the cheque
send the cheque back to the drawer for a second signature before it is collected
questions.e: "A/C Payee" instructs the collecting banker to collect the cheque only for the payee's own account, giving strong protection against misuse. It does not allow cash payment.

questions.s: A cheque dated for a day later than the day on which it is issued is
questions.e: A post-dated cheque carries a future date and cannot be paid before that date. An ante-dated cheque carries an earlier date than the day it is written.

questions.s: A cheque that has not been presented for payment for an unusually long period after its date, so that banks treat it as outdated, is a
questions.e: Banks refuse a cheque presented long after its date; it is then called stale and the drawer must issue a fresh one. A post-dated cheque is the opposite case, presented before its date.

questions.s: An endorsement that consists of the endorser's signature only, without naming the endorsee, is a
questions.e: A blank (general) endorsement is just a signature on the back, which makes the instrument payable to bearer. Naming the endorsee makes it a special (full) endorsement.

questions.s: An endorsement written as "Pay Ali only" is
questions.e: Words like "only" prevent any further negotiation, so the endorsement is restrictive. A sans recourse endorsement instead excludes the endorser's own liability.

questions.s: An endorser who writes "sans recourse" with his endorsement
o: makes the instrument payable to bearer
doubles his liability to the holder in due course
forbids all further transfer of the instrument
excludes his own liability to later holders if it is dishonoured
questions.e: "Sans recourse" means "without recourse to me": the endorser transfers the instrument but will not be liable if it is dishonoured. Forbidding further transfer is a restrictive endorsement.

questions.s: A holder in due course is a person who
o: took the instrument for value, in good faith, before it became due
obtained the instrument after its maturity date
received the instrument as a gift from the drawer
found the instrument and holds it as its bearer
questions.e: A holder in due course takes the instrument for consideration, without notice of defects and before maturity, and gets a title free from earlier defects. A finder or a person taking it as a gift does not give value.

questions.s: A bank draft is
o: a cheque drawn by a customer on his own account
a receipt for money kept in a fixed deposit
a written promise by a customer to repay a bank loan in monthly instalments
an order by a bank on its own branch to pay a stated sum
questions.e: A bank draft is issued by the bank, which orders its own branch elsewhere to pay; payment is therefore certain. An ordinary cheque depends on the customer having funds.

questions.s: Mudarabah in Islamic banking is a partnership in which
o: the bank leases an asset to a customer for a rent
one party provides capital and the other provides skill and management
both parties provide capital and manage the business together
the bank sells goods at cost plus an agreed profit
questions.e: In mudarabah, the capital provider (rabb-ul-maal) and the manager (mudarib) share profit in an agreed ratio, while a financial loss is borne by the capital provider unless the manager was negligent. Both partners providing capital describes musharakah.

questions.s: In Islamic banking, a sale in which the bank buys goods and sells them to the customer at cost plus a disclosed profit is
questions.e: Murabahah is a cost-plus sale with the cost and profit made known to the buyer, often on deferred payment. Ijarah is leasing, where the bank keeps ownership and charges rent.

questions.s: An Islamic financing contract in which the bank keeps ownership of an asset and lets the customer use it for an agreed rent is
questions.e: Ijarah is a lease: ownership stays with the lessor while the lessee pays rent for its use. Istisna is an order to manufacture an item for later delivery.

questions.s: In a salam contract,
o: both parties contribute capital and share profit and loss
the full price is paid in advance for goods to be delivered later
an asset is rented out and ownership never changes
goods are delivered at once and paid for later in instalments
questions.e: Salam is a forward sale with full advance payment, often used for agricultural produce, with quantity, quality and delivery date fixed. Delivery now with deferred payment is the opposite arrangement.

questions.s: Which of the following is an important function of a commercial bank in creating credit?
o: collecting income taxes for the government from all depositors at the end of the year
printing new notes whenever customers ask for loans
fixing the exchange rate of the rupee each morning
lending deposits so that loans return as new deposits in banks
questions.e: When a bank lends, the borrower's spending ends up as deposits in banks, which can be lent again; this multiplies deposits. Printing notes is reserved for the central bank.

questions.s: A person can insure a property only if he would suffer a financial loss from its damage. This is the principle of
questions.e: Insurable interest means the insured must stand to lose money if the subject matter is harmed; otherwise the policy would be a wager. Indemnity is about how much is paid after a loss.

questions.s: The principle of indemnity means that the insured
o: is restored to the same financial position as before the loss
is paid twice if he has two policies on one risk
can make a profit from an insurance claim
receives the sum insured even if the loss is smaller
questions.e: Indemnity limits compensation to the actual loss, so the insured neither gains nor loses. Receiving more than the loss would encourage people to cause losses.

questions.s: The principle of indemnity does not apply to
questions.e: A human life cannot be valued in money, so a life policy pays the agreed sum assured rather than an indemnity. Fire, marine and motor policies compensate only the actual loss.

questions.s: Bilal insured his shop for Rs. 2,000,000 with Company X and for Rs. 1,000,000 with Company Y. A fire causes a loss of Rs. 600,000. Under the principle of contribution, Company Y pays
questions.e: Under double insurance, insurers share the loss in proportion to their sums insured, 2 : 1. Company Y pays one-third of Rs. 600,000 = Rs. 200,000. Rs. 300,000 assumes an equal split, which ignores the different sums insured.

questions.s: Under the principle of proximate cause, an insurer pays a claim only if
o: the nearest effective cause of loss is a risk covered by the policy
the loss was caused by the insured's own deliberate act
the loss happened within one day of buying the policy
the insured has paid all premiums regularly for at least five years before the loss
questions.e: Proximate cause looks for the dominant, effective cause of the loss; if that cause is an insured peril, the claim is paid. A deliberate act by the insured is never covered.

questions.s: The amount paid by the insured to the insurer for cover against a risk is the
questions.e: The premium is the price of insurance. The policy is the document containing the contract, and a claim is the insured's demand after a loss.

questions.s: A life policy under which the sum assured is paid on the insured's death or at the end of a fixed period, whichever comes first, is
questions.e: An endowment policy combines protection and saving: it pays at maturity if the insured is alive, or earlier on death. A whole life policy pays only on death.

questions.s: When an insurer insures part of a large risk it has accepted with another insurer, it is called
questions.e: Reinsurance lets an insurer spread a risk too large for it alone. Double insurance is when the insured buys more than one policy on the same risk.

questions.s: In marine insurance, a loss caused by a deliberate sacrifice of part of the cargo to save the ship and the remaining cargo is
o: an uninsurable loss under every policy
a particular average loss borne by its owner alone
an actual total loss of the ship and cargo
a general average loss shared by all parties
questions.e: A sacrifice made for the common safety, such as jettisoning cargo in a storm, is a general average loss and is shared by all whose property was saved. A particular average loss is accidental partial damage that falls on the owner alone.

questions.s: The cheapest mode of transport for carrying bulky goods over long distances is usually
questions.e: Ships carry very large loads with low fuel and running cost per tonne, so water is the cheapest means for bulky goods. Air transport is the fastest but the most expensive.

questions.s: Ships that sail on fixed routes according to a published timetable are called
questions.e: Liners run regular scheduled services and carry goods of many shippers at fixed rates. Tramps have no fixed route or timetable and go wherever cargo is available.

questions.s: A bonded warehouse is used for storing
o: imported goods on which customs duty has not yet been paid
perishable goods such as fruit and meat at low temperature
goods kept by a bank as security for a loan
goods produced by a manufacturer for his own sale
questions.e: Imported goods may be kept in a bonded warehouse under customs control until the importer pays duty, often in instalments as he takes the goods out. Low-temperature storage is a cold storage.

questions.s: A warehouse warrant differs from a warehouse keeper's receipt because the warrant
o: is a document of title that can be transferred by endorsement
is issued only for goods stored in cold storage
must be returned to the warehouse within a week
is only an acknowledgement that goods have been received
questions.e: A warehouse warrant entitles its holder to the goods, so goods can be sold or pledged without moving them. A warehouse keeper's receipt only acknowledges receipt of goods and is not a document of title.

questions.s: A savings account is mainly meant for
o: traders who make many payments every day
companies that issue shares to the public
individuals who wish to save part of their income
governments that borrow from the central bank
questions.e: A savings account encourages thrift among individuals and pays a return, with some limits on withdrawals. Traders with frequent payments use current accounts.

questions.s: The maker of a promissory note is the person who
o: receives payment of the amount stated in the note
accepts the note on behalf of the payee
orders a bank to pay the amount on demand
promises to pay the amount stated in the note
questions.e: The maker signs the note and promises to pay; the payee is the person who receives the money. An order to a bank describes a cheque.

questions.s: The holder of a bill of exchange endorses it to Sana. Sana is called the
questions.e: The person who signs the endorsement is the endorser; the person to whom it is transferred is the endorsee. The drawer is the one who first wrote the bill.

questions.s: A cheque payable to "Imran or bearer" can be paid to
o: Imran only, after proving his identity
any person who presents it, without endorsement
questions.e: A bearer cheque is payable to whoever presents it, so it is risky if lost. An order cheque is payable only to the named payee or his order.

questions.s: Which of the following is NOT a negotiable instrument under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881?
questions.e: The Act names promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques as negotiable instruments. A fixed deposit receipt is only evidence of a deposit and cannot be passed on like a cheque.

questions.s: A bill of exchange drawn on 5 April is payable 60 days after date. Allowing days of grace, its date of maturity is
questions.e: Count 60 days after 5 April: 25 days left in April, 31 in May, so 4 more days reach 4 June. Adding three days of grace gives 7 June. 4 June is the date before the days of grace are added.

questions.s: A musharakah contract in Islamic banking is one in which
o: all partners provide capital and share profit and loss
the bank sells goods at cost plus a known profit
one partner provides capital and the other only labour
the price is paid in advance for future delivery
questions.e: In musharakah, all partners contribute capital; profit is shared in an agreed ratio and loss in proportion to capital. Capital from one side and labour from the other is mudarabah.

questions.s: The fastest mode of transport, suitable for perishable and valuable goods, is
questions.e: Air transport is the quickest, so it suits urgent, light, perishable or costly goods, despite its high cost. Water transport is cheap but slow.

questions.s: Crude oil and natural gas are most economically carried over land in large quantities by
questions.e: Pipelines move liquids and gases continuously at low running cost and with little loss. Trucks can carry oil but cost more per unit over long distances.

questions.s: The principle of contribution applies when
o: the same risk is insured with more than one insurer
the insured hides a material fact from the insurer
the insured has no financial interest in the property
the insurer reinsures part of the risk with another
questions.e: Under double insurance, each insurer contributes to the loss in proportion to its cover, and the insured still receives no more than the actual loss. Reinsurance is a separate arrangement between insurers.

questions.s: A warehouse helps to stabilise prices by
o: selling all stored goods below cost to customers during every season
fixing the prices of all goods it stores
storing goods when supply is high and releasing them when it is low
refusing to store goods during the harvest
questions.e: By holding stock in seasons of plenty and supplying it in seasons of shortage, warehouses smooth out supply and prices. Warehouses do not fix prices themselves.

questions.s: A ship that has no fixed route or timetable and carries cargo wherever it is available is a
questions.e: Tramps sail wherever there is cargo, often on charter. Liners follow fixed routes and timetables.

questions.s: The principle of utmost good faith in insurance requires that
o: the insured must buy a policy from one company only
the insurer pays every claim without any enquiry
the premium is the same for every type of risk
both parties disclose all material facts truthfully
questions.e: Insurance contracts are uberrimae fidei: the insured must reveal every fact that affects the risk, such as an existing illness, and the insurer must state the terms honestly. Hiding a material fact allows the insurer to avoid the contract.

questions.s: After paying a claim for a stolen car, the insurer takes over the insured's right to recover the car or damages from the thief. This is the principle of
questions.e: Subrogation passes the insured's rights against third parties to the insurer once the claim is paid, so the insured cannot be compensated twice. Contribution is about sharing a loss among several insurers.

questions.s: The four Ps of the marketing mix are
o: production, profit, packing and personal selling
questions.e: The marketing mix is the set of decisions a firm makes about its product, its price, where it is sold (place) and how it is communicated (promotion). Production and profit are not elements of the mix.

questions.s: In the marketing mix, "place" refers to
o: the location of the firm's head office building
the country where the raw materials are produced
the position of the product on a shop's shelf only
the channels through which goods reach customers
questions.e: Place covers distribution: wholesalers, retailers, transport and the points where buyers can obtain the product. It is not the address of the firm's office.

questions.s: Sorting products into classes of similar quality, such as grade A and grade B rice, is called
questions.e: Grading divides goods into lots of uniform quality so buyers can purchase by description. Branding gives a product a distinctive name or mark.

questions.s: A name, sign or symbol that identifies a firm's product and distinguishes it from competitors is a
questions.e: A brand creates identity and loyalty; when registered legally, it is protected as a trademark. A label of contents only gives information about what is inside.

questions.s: A firm introduces a new mobile phone at a low price to win a large share of the market quickly. This pricing policy is
questions.e: Penetration pricing sets a low initial price to attract many buyers fast. Skimming does the opposite: a high launch price aimed at buyers willing to pay more, lowered later.

questions.s: In the product life cycle, the stage in which sales grow slowly, promotion costs are high and profits are low or negative is the
questions.e: At introduction, few people know the product, so sales are low and spending on promotion is heavy. In the growth stage, sales rise rapidly and profits begin to grow.

questions.s: In the maturity stage of the product life cycle, a firm usually faces
o: rapidly rising sales with almost no competitors
falling sales and profits as the product is gradually withdrawn from the market
very low sales because few buyers know the product
peak sales with strong competition and pressure on prices
questions.e: At maturity, the market is saturated: sales reach their peak, many rivals compete and prices come under pressure. Falling sales and withdrawal belong to the decline stage.

questions.s: The purpose of advertising is mainly to
o: record the daily cash and credit sales of a business in its books
inform and persuade people to buy goods or services
transport goods to the buyer's door
insure goods against loss in transit
questions.e: Advertising is paid communication that creates awareness and demand. Transport and insurance are other aids to trade.

questions.s: In the AIDA model of advertising, the letters stand for
questions.e: A good advertisement first catches attention, then builds interest, creates desire and finally prompts action, such as buying. The other expansions are not the AIDA stages.

questions.s: Publicity differs from advertising mainly because publicity is
